en: And made the master who loosed him laugh.
A tested champion among beasts,
An heirloom left by the noble lord.
I will take hold of him by the collar;
Now that I, Bakai, am old,
I will loose my beloved Kumayyk
Upon the sly fox!
Today Kumayyk
Will rekindle aged Bakai’s
Extinguished fire,
And revive his lifeless soul.
In Bakai’s old age,
He will fatten me when I have grown lean,
Fill my empty stomach,
And satisfy my longing.
That Kumayyk is a champion,
I, a poor old soul, know well.
I have longed to loose Kumayyk,
To satisfy my desire fully,
And make myself young once more—
I have yearned for it.
In his old age, your khan and uncle
Will show what was not known,
Make you perceive what went unnoticed,
And have the straight road reconnoitered.
A gorge of towering black rock,
With birch and honeysuckle mingled within—
Facing that black cliff,
Cutting straight across the bend in the road,
To loose him upon the sly fox,
To have him sink his teeth in once,
Lion Bakai then went,
Leading Kumayyk.
The learned elder Bakai—
A sage mighty in what he knew—
Led him up onto a rugged saddle ridge.
Hero Bakai
Fastened and secured it once again:
The high-voiced doolbas drum,
Made from the hide of a bil;
When struck once with the axe,
The opposite mountain slope groaned.
When he came up onto the ridge,
Do not ask how the valiant man fared;
Your valiant uncle Bakai
Grasped the golden-cheeked battle-axe
And swung it back,
Making the doolbas ring out, ‘Kang!’
He struck it toward the middle.
From the spur of Bozala-Borchuk,
From the gray, knobby promontory,
From the ridge of Kara-Kyr,
From the place where he stood watch,
The fox darted forty fathoms.
Kumayyk went after him;
The fox fled, shimmering like a mirage,
And Kumayyk followed,
Running close upon his heels.
Behind him Kumayyk
Drew near, almost at his tail.
Seeing it, Bakai and Semetey
Shouted out in joy;
Your poor uncle Bakai
Raised the battle cry, “Manas!”
When they reached the downslope,
That bastard Kuutülkü
Dug in both his feet;
When Kumayyk braced like a warrior,
He seemed ready to take flight,
Driving himself straight down.
At the white peak by Ailanysh Spring,
Kuutülkü’s stratagems ran out,
And he fled six circuits around it.
At Zheti-Bulak in Zherge-Tal,
Kuutülkü proved resourceful
And fled seven circuits around it.
Kumayyk ranged over the ridges,
Pressing Kuutülkü hard.
The fox kept on,
Watching for a gully where he could escape.
When he saw how the fox fled,
Fearing it would reach its lair at once,
Fearing it might somehow escape,
Bakai shouted in fury,
Raising the Bloodthirsty One’s battle cry.
He lashed Kökcholok beneath him
From side to side with his whip,
Spurred him on both flanks,
And shouted in fury.
Sacred Khan Bakai
Bent down the tops of the birches,
Startling the sly fox,
Making his horse pound along,
Stretching him out in pursuit;
Your uncle Lord Bakai
Sent him galloping with great bounds.
The ground crumbled under his tread;
Your accomplished uncle Bakai
Drove straight at the fox.
The place toward which the fox fled
Was a reedy ravine and gorge.
To slip inside it,
That accursed Kuutülkü
Strove with all his might
To mislead Kumayyk behind him
And get past.
Hurrying in alarm and panting,
Your uncle Bakai lamented:
“God surely exists, Kumayyk!
Why do you run with such stiff joints—
Has God struck you down?!
Unable to understand your fitful condition,
Now that I am old, Kumayyk,
Or has God struck me down?!
When my lord, the gray wolf, died,
I was the one who herded camels,
And you were the one left grieving,
Your ribs battered open!
If you do not heed the tears in my eyes,
If you do not bite and bring me the fox,
I will club your head open;
I, Bakai, will not remain alive,
But will strike myself down.
I, this wretched bastard, will die
And behold the face of Judgment Day!”
Your noble uncle Bakai—
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of an eye,
At the reedy hollow in the gorge,
Your accomplished uncle Bakai
Suddenly appeared before him.
When the fox saw Khan Bakai,
The poor creature darted aside
And flashed toward the top
Of the black cliff above the gorge.
Bakai stood shouting,
Pleading with the one God;
Kumayyk came racing,
His ears laid flat to the ground.
As the fox was about to leap
Over a black rock as large as a house,
Kumayyk raced up and caught
The fox doomed to an unclean death.
He passed over the ridge,
And, gripping the fox in his teeth,
Flung it over a black rock
As tall as a camel.
When it struck, the fox split apart.
Ah, Kumayyk, wondrous creature—
His prowess was revealed!
Bakai came racing over,
Offering praises to Kumayyk!
“My beloved Kumayyk,
My champion left by the lion!
Today all my pent-up grief has opened,
And all my sorrow has scattered!
Joined with me when you were no bigger than a louse,
My beloved Kumayyk,
United with me when you were no bigger than a thumb.
On the plain where you chased the fox,
May the entrusted life of your uncle,
Lion Bakai, be your sacrifice!
Your capable uncle Bakai
His white saber with a mottled neck.
Hurriedly then,
Took it from his side.
Bakai cut its windpipe,
And performed a wondrous rite.
The expert leopard Bakai
Skinned the fox into a whole pelt;
His anger settled and he grew calm.
Without speaking a word or saying a thing,
Your aged uncle became absorbed in his work.
“Oh, do not be offended, my child, do not be offended!
There are watchmen farther on;
I will accept what you have said!
If I return to Talas,
I will have it made into a hat
For my wretched son Baitailak!”
Having skinned the fox and carried out his design,
Poor Bakai made a feast
For the ravens and magpies.
He swiftly invoked Babedin,
And, for the sake of lion Manas,
Named and dedicated a horse, beginning with Aituyak.
Semetey, whom he had led with him,
Prepared to begin the reconnaissance;
He pleaded with Semetey,
The sole support he had:
“Ah, my beloved Semetey,
The omen is auspicious, the undertaking good.
We shall tread upon the head
Of that lordly Kongurbai;
If mighty Allah supports us,
We shall make the infidels howl
And scatter all four kinds of their livestock!
We shall bring them boundless sorrow;
We shall raid and seize the herds at Keng-Shor
From that swine,
The khan of the Kechil, and make him grieve!
We shall make slaughter into a spectacle;
Ah, my beloved champion,
We shall avenge many wrongs!
That would-be hero, Lord Kong,
We shall tread upon his brow!
If mighty Allah grants us a path,
We shall scatter all his wealth!
The one you will grapple with is the Kakanchin,
The one you will oppose is Bakburchun;
Lungtu, Kengtu, and Dyngsha—
While Manas was alive,
I encountered all these men!
My valiant morning star, listen well:
The road to Beijing has five branches.
In my old age you make me lead the road,
And have heaped hardship on this wretched head!
When I seek a night’s lodging, you make me a guest;
In your uncle Bakai’s old age,
You would have me begin the tale!”
Over there, hazy and angular in the distance,
Ending in a dim and shadowed point—
For a man riding a powerful horse,
My mighty champion, listen well:
That is a desert forty days across;
The land looming beyond it
Is the country of the Manchus.
That white ridge beneath forked clouds
Is Chong-Shangkai itself.
The sight of it once stirred my heart;
I beat those people black as coal
And took tribute from them!
While the learned Manas lived,
Alas for those woeful days,
I used to do whatever I knew how to do!
Whoever offered resistance,
I would seize and cut down!
I would cast humiliation upon them like a flock of sheep;
From the graceful beauties—
With thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
With darting black eyes,
Crimson dresses and moon-slim waists—
I would take tribute in daughters,
And satisfy my desire in this way.
While my lion was alive,
This was a land where I went as governor,
A land where I took its gold and silver
As tax and tribute.
On the face of that slope
Stands a building raised high across it.
When this campaign comes to mind,
My soul cannot be held within a hand!
Thinking often of former times,
My beard has turned white;
When I think of them, I grieve!
My old fury is stirred,
My beloved colt,
